The Board

The Guarantee, the Hike, and the Handover

The war in Ukraine and the security guarantee designed to end it, the Federal Reserve's December meeting after October inflation rose again, and Houston and Texas in the weeks between an election that flipped the state and the January days when power actually changes hands.

Scroll

Donetsk region

A war of substations and calendars.

The front barely moves. The grid, the guarantee, and the dates in December and January are where the war is actually being decided.

Photograph via The Insight International. General Oleksandr Syrskyi walks a front-line trench in Donetsk region, April 2026. The front he commands seized and lost ground in October and ended the month behind where it started on the other side.

What's Moved

The November 25 data settled December’s direction and shrank its tail: core PCE rose 3.3 percent over the year, third-quarter growth was revised up to 4.3 percent, and weekly jobless claims fell to 189,000. A half-point hike, openly discussed ten days ago, is nearly gone from futures pricing.

The guarantee at the center of the Ukraine talks got harder, not softer. As described on November 25, it would need approval from Congress, then from Russia, and a president confident it would never be used, in that order.

The one product of the Abu Dhabi talks moved toward execution: a multi-stage prisoner exchange that could start in late November or early December. No second round of talks has a date.

Brent crude fell to $89.37 on November 23, its lowest since August, then rose for two days to settle at $94.61 on November 25, up 3.5 percent that day, on claimed attacks on Saudi Arabia’s Ras Tanura refinery. The claims are unconfirmed. The price is real, and OPEC+ meets on November 29.

Houston entered the bidding for the Essence Festival this week, confirming talks the day after New Orleans lost it. No price has been disclosed, and the mayor stood with airport workers the same day because his own August wage order is still not being paid.

In Texas, nothing changed hands. The fights that decide January moved instead: a court race over Houston’s immigration order, a school board planning its own exit, and an ERCOT filing due December 10.

Verdict

Three questions run through this report. What is the security guarantee for Ukraine actually worth, as it is now designed? What does the Federal Reserve do on December 9, now that the last data before the meeting has landed? And in Texas, who holds power in the weeks between an election and an inauguration?

The answers rhyme. On each board, the loud event has already happened, and the real decision sits somewhere quieter, later, and harder to move.

The guarantee Kyiv is being asked to trade land for cannot be delivered by the men offering it. The December hike is priced as settled, but the vote has not been taken and the data that could change it lands the day after. The Texas sweep is final on paper and powerless until January, while the outgoing government’s court filings, contracts, and queue decisions are being made now.

Leverage, this month, belongs to whoever can wait: Moscow, which holds the ground being negotiated over; a Federal Reserve committee that meets on its own calendar; and in Texas, the institutions whose terms run past the inauguration.

Chapter One

The War on the Ground

The map stayed still this week. The grid war did not, and the insurers have already delivered their verdict on the talks.

The front did not move this week. The war did.

Ukraine’s General Staff counted 203 combat engagements in the 24 hours reported on November 25, with the heaviest fighting again on the Pokrovsk direction. Daily counts have stayed at that level all month without producing a breakthrough on any axis.

Tempo is not progress. In October, Russian forces seized about 140 square kilometers and lost about 167, a net loss of about 27 square kilometers, mapped by the Institute for the Study of War from geolocated footage.

It was the second straight month of net loss, and the loss came in Donetsk, the province Moscow says it must have in full before any ceasefire.

Ukraine’s General Staff says Russian losses in the first 25 days of November exceeded the October record it reported. Those are Kyiv’s figures, not independently verified, and this report treats them as a claim about tempo, not a ledger.

The war that is moving is the one against the grid. ACLED, which tracks political violence event by event, found Russian strikes on Ukrainian energy infrastructure nearly doubled in the second half of 2026.

The aim point moved too, from the front and Kyiv toward substations in central and western Ukraine. One November attack left more than 600,000 people in Dnipropetrovsk region without power.

A substation is cheaper than a town. Destroying one raises the cost of winter for millions of people without spending a single infantryman, and it is aimed at the negotiating table as much as at the grid.

Kyiv is striking back at Russia’s fuel system, and on November 24 President Putin publicly promised a response, saying Ukraine keeps attacking Russian refineries despite an American request to stop. He also acknowledged export restrictions and subsidies to steady Russia’s own fuel market.

The money under the war moved in Russia’s favor this year. A European Commission report circulated this week put Russian crude export revenue for January through September at $102 billion, already above the $101 billion earned in all of 2025, with China and India taking 85 percent of exports.

Higher oil prices fund the attacker here. They do not tighten the vise.

The insurers price the sea war separately. War-risk premiums for voyages to the CPC terminal at Novorossiysk cluster at 7.5 to 10 percent of hull value, with upper-end quotes at 20 percent, against a quarter to a third of one percent before the invasion.

Romania and Bulgaria coastal transits still price at 0.4 to 1 percent, the one corridor under the roughly 2 percent level brokers cite as the line where trade normalizes. CMA CGM added a war-risk surcharge of $35 per container on Black Sea cargo from November 9.

That spread is the physical verdict on the talks. Diplomats can announce progress. A shipowner still pays twenty times the peacetime price to load oil on the Black Sea.

Chapter Two

The Guarantee and the Table

A prisoner exchange is moving. Everything it was supposed to unlock is not, and the guarantee at the center of the talks is designed so the country it deters can veto it.

The last negotiating round was in Abu Dhabi on November 10 and 11. It produced one agreement, on a prisoner exchange, and that agreement was in principle only.

Since then the exchange has been the only moving part. Ukrainian officials said on November 25 that a multi-stage exchange could begin in late November or early December and involve more than 1,000 people. President Zelensky had put the possible scale at 1,000 to 1,200 people on each side.

An exchange is verifiable, photographable, and costs neither side a meter of ground. It is what low-trust negotiations produce first, in this war and in most others.

Everything else is stuck where Abu Dhabi left it. Russia demands that Ukraine withdraw from the part of Donbas it still holds before any ceasefire. Ukraine holds about a fifth of Donetsk province, the fortress belt Russia has failed to take since 2022.

Moscow is not only negotiating a line. Its delegation revived Russia’s December 2021 demand for a new European security arrangement, rolling NATO back toward its 1997 footprint. The subject of the talks, if Moscow gets its way, is the continent, not the ceasefire.

Against that demand sits the guarantee, and this week its design came into the open. The Institute for the Study of War described the American proposal on November 25: an Article 5-style guarantee that would be considered only after approval by the United States Congress, approval by Russia, a presidential judgment that it serves American interests, and agreement on the wider European security architecture.

Read that chain slowly. The guarantee Kyiv would receive in exchange for land requires the consent of the country the guarantee is meant to deter.

Jared Kushner said over the weekend that Moscow is now comfortable with Article 5-style guarantees. Comfort is cheap when the design hands you a veto over whether the guarantee ever exists.

Washington holds a second, quieter lever over Kyiv. Zelensky said on November 24 that the United States continues to delay delivery of Patriot interceptor missiles, including missiles already paid for by partners. Patriot is the only system Ukraine has that can intercept Russian ballistic missiles.

On November 25 the State Department approved a possible $621.9 million sale of F-16 maintenance equipment and services to Ukraine. Sustainment moves. The interceptors that decide whether Kyiv’s power stations survive the winter are the item being held.

Europe’s lever is money, and it is being assembled in Brussels. On November 18 the European Commission proposed a loan of up to 45 billion euros for Ukraine in 2027, split between up to 25 billion in military assistance and up to 20 billion in budget support, covering two-thirds of an estimated 70 billion euro financing gap.

The loan is limited-recourse: Ukraine repays the principal only once Russia pays reparations. It sits on top of a 90 billion euro support loan already agreed for 2026 and 2027, and it still needs approval from the European Parliament and the member states, several of which do not want to guarantee it.

The great powers met without Ukraine or Europe at all on November 19, when Presidents Trump, Xi, and Putin sat down for 90 minutes in Shenzhen, on the sidelines of the APEC summit. Xi hosted. They agreed to open a dialogue on reducing nuclear risks and to plan increased supplies of refined petroleum products.

No Ukrainian or European sat at that table. The architecture Moscow wants to renegotiate is now being discussed in rooms Europe does not sit in, and the petroleum pledge ties the war talks directly to the oil market the Fed is watching.

Trump added his own pressure this week, in both directions. On November 24 he laughed off the idea that peace would come by January and refused a deadline. On November 26 he posted that he had told Putin to pull back military aggression across Europe so a deal could be made quickly, calling the war a complete bloodbath.

A deadline the mediator will not enforce is not a deadline. It is pressure on the side that needs the mediator, which is Kyiv.

Chapter Three

The Fed and the Price of Money

December's question is size, not direction. The last data before the meeting landed on November 25, and the data that could change the answer lands the day after the vote.

The Federal Reserve meets on December 8 and 9. The question is no longer whether it raises rates. It is by how much, and what it promises next.

The chair is Kevin Warsh, confirmed by the Senate in May by 54 votes to 45, the most divided confirmation in the Fed’s history. He succeeded Jerome Powell when Powell’s term as chair ended, and he inherited inflation that has run above the 2 percent target for close to six years.

Warsh’s committee raised rates in September, the first increase since July 2023, taking the target range to 3.75 to 4.00 percent. In October it held, by 10 votes to 2.

Both dissenters, Governor Lisa Cook and Cleveland President Beth Hammack, wanted a hike at that meeting. The October minutes, released November 18, said almost all participants judged further increases likely in coming months, and a couple of participants raised the possibility of a move larger than a quarter point in December.

Governor Christopher Waller set a public test on November 10. If October core consumer inflation came in at about 0.3 percent or higher, he said, a half-point hike should be considered, and settling for a quarter point would put the Fed’s credibility at risk.

The data met his test exactly. Core consumer prices rose 0.3 percent in October, the third straight month at that pace. Headline prices rose 0.4 percent.

Then, on November 25, the last reports before the meeting landed together. Core PCE, the price measure the Fed targets, rose 3.3 percent over the year to October, up from 3.1 percent in September and above the 3.2 percent forecast. Headline PCE rose 3.8 percent. Brent crude settled at $94.61 a barrel on November 25, down from $104.77 on November 2.

Third-quarter growth was revised up to 4.3 percent annualized, from a 3.4 percent first estimate. The economy the Fed is trying to slow is, on the revised numbers, growing fast.

The labor market agrees. Employers added 165,000 jobs in October, and the two prior months were revised up by a combined 84,000. The three-month average gain is 137,000, up from 83,000 over six months. Hiring re-accelerated; it did not stall.

Weekly jobless claims, the fastest labor signal and the one barely revised later, fell to 189,000 in the week ending November 21. Firms are not laying people off.

Factories confirm it from the ground. The Institute for Supply Management’s October survey put new orders at 55.5 and production at a five-year high, with prices paid at 75.2, a level that means most firms are paying more for inputs.

The physical layer agrees. Refineries ran at 97.5 percent of capacity in the week reported November 25, and distillate stocks sit 6 percent below their five-year average. Diesel, at $5.70 a gallon against $3.64 for gasoline, is the tight product and the inflation channel to watch.

Markets have done the committee’s arithmetic. Pricing for a quarter-point hike on December 9 runs from roughly nine chances in ten to near certainty, depending on the venue and the day. The half-point tail has shrunk to nearly nothing in futures, after an equity selloff made a panic move look worse than a steady one.

One calendar fact disciplines all of this. November’s consumer price report is published on December 10, the day after the vote. The committee will decide on October’s inflation, the November 25 PCE report, and the December 4 jobs report, and on nothing newer.

Markets closed Thursday for Thanksgiving, so the last full snapshot is Wednesday’s close. The S&P 500 ended at 7,183, down a quarter percent on the day. The ten-year Treasury yield ended at 4.85 percent. Brent crude settled at $94.61 a barrel, up 3.5 percent on the day, on claimed attacks on Saudi Arabia’s Ras Tanura refinery that no one has confirmed, and West Texas Intermediate settled at $83.68.

That $10.93 spread between the two crudes is Texas money. It is also the Fed’s problem in miniature: the inflation impulse is arriving through energy and supply, which a rate hike cannot pump out of the ground, into a committee that has decided credibility requires it to try anyway.

Chapter Four

Houston

Houston first. A festival bid with no price, a wage order nobody is enforcing, a court race against an inauguration, and the one institution in the city that elections do not touch.

Houston first. The city’s one new move this week was a bid, and it came with no price attached.

On November 24, Sundial Media Group announced the Essence Festival of Culture will leave New Orleans after 31 years, its contract expired and negotiations over money and unpaid vendors stalled. On November 25, Mayor John Whitmire and Houston First chief Michael Heckman confirmed Houston is in direct talks to take it. Atlanta and Memphis are bidding too.

The festival has reportedly brought more than 400,000 people to New Orleans every July 4 weekend in recent years, and Houston hosted it once before, in 2006, after Katrina. What killed the New Orleans deal is reported to be an ask of $10 million to $12 million in incentives. Houston has disclosed no terms, no venue, and no start date.

The money, if it comes, will not come from the general fund. This spring Houston and Houston First sold about $1.38 billion in hotel occupancy tax bonds for the convention center expansion. The festival decision is a hotel-tax decision, which means it can be made with far less public process than a budget item of the same size.

The same day, Whitmire stood with airport workers at Bush Intercontinental because his own order is not being obeyed. In August he raised the airport wage floor to $20 an hour, rising to $21 on January 1. At least four contractors have not paid it. An executive order the mayor cannot enforce against contractors is a press release with a signature, and November 24 was the day that became visible.

The month’s largest Houston fight is in court, on a calendar the mayor does not control. On November 6, three days after the statewide election flipped Texas, Whitmire ordered Houston police to contact federal immigration agents only when a person is already being jailed on new charges and has a confirmed federal warrant hit.

On November 13, outgoing Attorney General Ken Paxton’s office moved for summary judgment in Fort Bend County in its suit, opened in April, to block the order under SB 4, the 2017 law that bars cities from limiting immigration enforcement. Paxton leaves office in January. The incoming attorney general won on the other side of the issue. The city’s strategy is written in its own filings and statements: outlast him.

City Attorney Arturo Michel then blocked the durability play. On November 17 he ruled that a council ordinance writing Whitmire’s order into law, word for word, was unlawful, and Whitmire backed him in open session. The policy stays an executive order: entirely the mayor’s, revocable by any successor, and dependent on a court clock and an inauguration date rather than on law the city passed itself.

Harris County is running the same play at county scale. The outgoing Commissioners Court adopted the election canvass on November 12 and, on November 19, renewed the county’s immigrant legal services fund for all of 2027, about $1.07 million across four legal aid groups, on a 2 to 1 vote. County Judge-elect Letitia Plummer, who takes office January 1, announced her transition team on November 19. The old court is locking in next year’s commitments before she sits.

The school district is doing the reverse: unwinding itself. The state-appointed board running Houston ISD said this month it is working itself out of a job and planning for elected trustees to be ready by mid-January.

It is still spending while it exits, approving a $92 million career center contract the same month. Superintendent Mike Miles told district advisers he expects to leave once a new state education commissioner is named. His contract runs to June 2030, and removing him without cause could cost up to $924,000.

The Port, as usual, is the institution none of this touches. October was its biggest October on record: 415,326 containers, up 14 percent, with a record 3.76 million containers for the year through October.

On November 10 the Port Commission approved a 2027 budget of $569 million in operations and $397 million in capital spending, projecting about 4.6 million containers next year. Record volume, appointed commission, no election. The Port is what Houston’s other institutions are not: settled.

Chapter Five

Texas

Then Texas. A sweep that changed every office and one chamber, a calendar that gives the losers seven more weeks of signatures, and a grid queue that will not be sorted this winter.

Then Texas, where the election was a sweep and the government has not changed.

On November 3, Democrats won every statewide executive office on the ballot. Gina Hinojosa beat Greg Abbott for governor, 52.8 percent to 45.7 percent, the first Democratic win since Ann Richards. James Talarico beat Ken Paxton for the United States Senate, 55.1 percent to 43.0 percent. Vikki Goodwin took the lieutenant governorship, and Democrats flipped the Texas House to 83 seats against 67.

One chamber did not move. Republicans held the Texas Senate, 19 to 12, without a single seat changing parties. That one line of arithmetic governs everything that follows.

The calendar governs the rest. The Legislature convenes on January 12. Hinojosa is sworn in on January 19, a week later. Harris County’s new judge takes office January 1. For the next seven weeks, Texas is governed by the people who lost, advised by the people who won, and both sides know it.

The fights of the transition are therefore about what can be locked in before January, and what can be blocked after it. The Senate confirms the governor’s appointees, including the Public Utility Commission, which regulates the parts of the electricity business the state can actually set prices for. Goodwin, a Democrat, will preside over that Republican Senate with only the powers its rules give her, and the Senate writes its own rules.

That is why the campaign promise to freeze residential electricity rates runs into a wall the campaign did not mention. Most Texans in the competitive market buy power from retailers the state does not price. A governor’s reach runs through transmission and distribution rate cases at a commission she cannot quickly restaff. The promise names an outcome. The institution holds a narrower tool.

The grid’s real queue tells the same story in numbers. ERCOT’s Batch Zero process, which replaced project-by-project studies in July, classifies 204 large-load projects totaling 66.4 gigawatts as base load, with a further 127.9 gigawatts in studied load that cannot be energized before January 1, 2028 on the current filing. The headline queue numbers quoted in public, above 400 gigawatts, are requests. The studied numbers are the board.

Five developers have complained to the utility commission about the process. On November 19 the commission dismissed two of the complaints on a filing deadline, and its chairman has targeted March 31, 2027 for resolving the rest.

ERCOT told the commission on November 6 that it has no official peak forecast for this winter, because the Batch Zero load values are not final. The grid operator cannot say how much power Texas will need at its peak until the queue is sorted, and the queue will not be sorted this winter.

Winter risk itself is genuinely two-sided. The North American reliability assessment published November 18 lowered ERCOT’s overall risk rating, crediting 1.7 gigawatts of new gas generation and about 3.5 gigawatts of new batteries, while its own peak-hour numbers worsened: the probability of an energy emergency rose to 2.7 percent and the reserve margin thinned to 34.8 percent. Both halves are in the same document. Anyone quoting only one is selling something.

In the House, the transition is furthest along. Representative Senfronia Thompson of Houston, the chamber’s dean, is the only remaining candidate for Speaker, claiming 90 pledged votes against the 76 she needs, and she has named six former Speakers to her transition team. If the pledges hold on January 12, Houston holds the gavel in the one chamber that flipped.

Chapter Six

Two Rival Reads

Is the wait a strategy or a trap? Two coherent answers built on the same facts, and the evidence that separates them.

The wait is the strategy The strongest case that nothing is stuck is that waiting is what winning looks like from the side holding the asset.

Russia holds the Donbas ground under discussion, collects record crude revenue at $95 oil, and pays for its position in a currency, winter, that renews itself. Every week without a settlement is a week the guarantee gets more conditional and Ukraine’s grid gets weaker.

In Washington, pricing has already done part of the committee’s work: mortgage and credit costs moved before the vote, which is tightening delivered early, even if pricing can reverse in a day. In Texas, the incoming government inherits a Senate it cannot move and a queue it did not create, and gets to govern against both rather than answer for either.

Under this read, the frozen board is not a failure of the talks, the Fed, or the transition. It is the distribution of leverage, accurately priced by everyone involved.

The wait is the trap The strongest case the other way is that every actor waiting is waiting on a date that can hurt them.

Russia’s October map is a net loss in the very province it demands, its refining system is being degraded by strikes its president publicly had to answer for on November 24, and its own fuel market needs export restrictions and subsidies to stay steady. Time is not free for Moscow either. It is priced in refineries, in fuel, and in a map that moved backward while the talks were running.

The Fed’s wait is shorter and sharper. It votes on December 9 and gets November’s inflation the next morning. If that print is hot, the quarter point becomes the credibility story of the winter, and the committee will have spent its meeting proving the opposite of what it intended.

In Texas, the outgoing government’s seven weeks of signatures cut both ways: every lock-in is a target. A court loss on the immigration order, a Batch Zero ruling the new government can campaign against, and a Senate that must publicly block a governor elected by seven points are all costs that arrive in January, itemized.

Under this read, the board is not frozen. It is loaded, and the dates in December and January are when it moves all at once.

What decides between the reads is observable: whether November inflation on December 10 makes the December decision look behind, and whether the Fort Bend court rules before the inauguration makes its ruling moot.

Chapter Seven

Scenarios

Three futures, each with one observable event that confirms it and one that kills it. None is presented as certain.

A track, not theater. The Abu Dhabi channel becomes a real negotiation: a four-way round is announced with a date, and Europe is in the room. Confirm: a dated four-way meeting announced before January 1, with European participation named. Kill: January arrives with no meeting date set, whatever the envoys say.

The hike that starts an argument. The Fed raises a quarter point on December 9, and the November consumer price report the next morning makes the move look small within 24 hours. Confirm: November core consumer inflation, published December 10, rises 0.3 percent or more for the month. Kill: it rises 0.2 percent or less, and January pricing settles at one more quarter point or none.

The lock-in is tested early. Houston’s immigration order becomes the first ruling of the Texas transition. Confirm: the Fort Bend County court rules on the state’s summary judgment motion before January 19. Kill: no ruling by inauguration day, which leaves the incoming attorney general free to drop the case and makes the mayor’s calendar strategy the winning one by default.

Chapter Eight

Watchlist

Five developments that would change the analysis.

December 4, the November jobs report. The last data the Fed gets before it votes. A strong print locks the quarter point and revives the half-point argument in the room. A weak one is the only realistic path to a hold.

December 9 and 10, in that order. The Fed decides on the 9th and learns November’s inflation on the 10th. ERCOT’s Batch Zero filings also land in this window. Two of the report’s three boards move within 48 hours, and the order of events is the risk.

The prisoner exchange. If named lists are published and buses actually move, Abu Dhabi was a track. If late November and early December pass with statements only, it was theater, and the guarantee chain is the real state of the talks.

November 29, OPEC+. A quota decision that holds Brent in the mid-$90s funds Russia and feeds the Fed’s problem. A breakdown toward the $60s reverses both at once and rewrites the winter for Moscow, Houston refiners, and the December dot plot’s sequel in January.

January 12 and January 19 in Austin. The Legislature convenes first, under a Houston Speaker if the pledges hold, and the new governor arrives a week later. What the Senate’s rules do to the lieutenant governor, and what the Fort Bend court has or has not done by then, will say more about Texas power than the election did.
